text: The Design Museum of Chicago, formerly known as the Chicago Design Museum, is a non-profit 501(c)(3) organization founded by Tanner Woodford in 2012 as a pop-up museum, hosting exhibitions in various Chicago venues during 2012 and 2013. Following a successful Kickstarter campaign in 2014, it opened a permanent location in the Block 37 building. In late 2018, the museum relocated to Expo 72 at 72 E. Randolph St. Its mission is to "educate, inspire, and foster innovation through design." The museum operates through collaborative, community-based programs, largely dependent on local volunteers for exhibit design, curation, registration, marketing, and other core functions, with its foundation rooted in the visions and labor of these volunteers. It promotes free, open, and honest engagement with diverse audiences through a permanent collection, rotating exhibitions, and educational programming. Exhibitions cover a broad, cross-disciplinary definition of design, including graphic design, architecture, urban planning, interior design, and systems thinking. In 2021, the museum partnered with the Chicago Department of Public Health and the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events to commission over 80 local artists to create original art exploring themes of health, vitality, community, and vaccine distribution, which is displayed on print and digital billboards across Chicago neighborhoods and on social media. Artists in the campaign include Afrokilla, Alice Hargrave, Anthony Lewellen, Ashley Lin, Bob Faust, CZR PRZ, Carlos Rolón, Carlos Segura, Cody Hudson, Cristi López, Dan Grzeca, Dont Fret, Elloo, Emmy Star Brown, Esther Garcia, Gabriel Villa, Hector Duarte, Jason Pickleman, Jeff Zimmerman, Johnny Sampson, Kelly Knaga, Langston Allston, Lori Seidemann, Moises Salazar, Penny Pinch, Pouya Ahmadi, Rosemary Holiday Hall, Rubén Aguirre, Shannon Downey, Sonnenzimmer, Substance Collective, The Kid From Pilsen, Thomas Williams, Unyimeabasi Udoh, William J. O’Brien, and Won Kim. The Great Ideas of Humanity series features contemporary artists responding to quotes by scientists, philosophers, and academics, acknowledging the globalization of ideas and inspired by Chicago's Container Corporation of America's Great Ideas of Western Man campaign. Advertisements from this series have been displayed downtown on bus rapid transit stanchions and in Hong Kong at the Business of Design Week InnoTech Design Expo. Contributors include Matthew Hoffman (Susan B. Anthony), Andy Gregg (Mary Wollstonecraft), Renata Graw (Hypatia), 50,000feet (Goethe), Margot Harrington (Sojourner Truth), Cocu Liu (George Sand), Pouya Ahmadi (Rumi), Patternbase (Lucy Larcom), Eileen Tjan (Goethe), Kimberly Terzis (Anne Sophie Swetchine), Alexander Skoirchet (Buddha), Marcus Norman (Lucy Larcom), Tanner Woodford (Edith Wharton), Veronica Corzo-Duchardt (Goethe), LaShun Tines (Frederick Douglass), Matthew Terdich (Benjamin Franklin), Bibliothèque (Alfred North Whitehead), Hugh Dubberly (John Dewey), and Ivan Chermayeff (Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.). The Chicago Design Market is a rotating series of pop-up shops on the third floor of Block 37, where small emerging artists and established businesses share space. Shops are not charged for utilities or rent; instead, the museum takes a sales commission, enabling small designers like Aviate Press to market while allowing larger businesses like Cards Against Humanity to experiment. Selected stores include Cards Against Humanity, The Colossal Shop, You Are Beautiful, Fourneau Bread Oven, School of the Art Institute of Chicago, Resketch, Sweetwater Foundation, Shawnimals, Aviate Press, AIA Chicago, Dock 6 Collective, and mercer & winnie. The Design Pack is a Cards Against Humanity expansion pack featuring 30 illustrated cards interpreting George Carlin's 1972 monologue "Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television," with all proceeds benefiting the Design Museum of Chicago; sales exceeded $130,000 in its first few days. Similar non-profit packs by Cards Against Humanity have raised nearly millions for DonorsChoose.org, the Wikimedia Foundation, and the Sunlight Foundation. Contributors to the Design Pack include Laura Park, Shawna X, Chad Kouri, Susan Kare, Yann Legendre, Paula Scher, Jay Ryan, Mike McQuade, Paul Octavious, Erik Spiekermann, Max Temkin, Debbie Millman, Art Paul, Simon Whybray, Mike Mitchell, Scott Thomas, Matthew Terdich, Jez Burrows, Jason Polan, Jessica Hische, Cody Hudson, Nick Adam, Matthew Hoffman, Magdalena Wistuba + Anna Mort, Eric Hu, Olly Moss, Tanner Woodford, Milton Glaser, and Sonnenzimmer. The museum’s current logo was designed by the Chicago-based Substance Collective, inspired by the city’s urban grid and the interconnectivity of streets, thoroughfares, blocks, and neighborhoods. After nearly fourteen years, Tanner Woodford stepped down as executive director on January 31, 2026, and continued as founder and board member.
